title: 04 — Building MCP Servers and Clients
html:
04 — Building MCP Servers and Clients

The one idea: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard plug between AI applications and your systems. Write a tool once as an MCP server, and any MCP-capable client (desktop assistants, IDEs, agents, your own app) can discover and call it. In 2026 the protocol moved to a stateless core, so build servers that answer each request on its own.

1. What it is

Part Meaning
Host or client The AI application (an assistant, an IDE, your agent) that connects to servers
Server Your program that exposes capabilities
Tools Functions the model can call. Each has a name, a description and an inputSchema (JSON Schema), and can return text and structuredContent
Resources Data the client can read (files, records), addressed by URI
Prompts Reusable prompt templates the server offers
Transport How messages travel: stdio (a local process) or Streamable HTTP (a remote server)
Messages JSON-RPC 2.0: methods such as tools/list and tools/call

Current version, checked 2026-10-27: the specification dated 2026-07-28 is the current release. It moves MCP to a stateless request and response core. According to the official blog, it brings multi-round-trip requests, header-based routing, cacheable list results, hardened authorization, a formal extensions framework, and updated SDKs (TypeScript, Python, Go and C# were updated alongside it).

Migration write-ups describe these breaking changes. They are secondary sources, so confirm them in the official changelog:

  • the initialize handshake removed, with protocol version and capabilities carried on every request,
  • the Mcp-Session-Id header removed,
  • list results cacheable,
  • some request headers made mandatory on Streamable HTTP,
  • sampling, roots and logging deprecated rather than removed.

MCP is now governed under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, alongside the A2A protocol (05).

2. Why it matters

  • One integration, many clients: your fund-data lookup works in a desktop assistant, an IDE and your own agent without rewriting.
  • A governed surface: tools are typed contracts you can review, version and secure (07).
  • Stateless servers scale behind ordinary load balancers, like any web API.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Message flow

---
title: MCP tool discovery and call
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host (AI app)
    participant M as Model
    participant S as MCP server
    H->>S: tools/list
    S-->>H: tool names, descriptions, input schemas
    H->>M: user question + tool definitions
    M-->>H: call get_nav(isin, date)
    H->>S: tools/call get_nav
    S-->>H: content + structuredContent (or isError)
    H->>M: tool result
    M-->>H: final answer

3.2 Designing good tools

  • One clear job per tool, with a name and description written for the model: when to use it, and what it returns.
  • Tight schemas: required fields, formats, enums, and additionalProperties: false.
  • Return errors as results (isError: true) with a helpful message, so the model can correct itself.
  • Idempotent and read-only by default. Put side-effect tools behind confirmation.
  • Stateless: if you need state across calls, return an explicit handle the client passes back as an argument.
  • Security: authenticate every request. Accept only tokens issued for your server, never pass a client's token through, and run with the caller's permissions (OL 18).

3.3 Building a server

Python with the official SDK (pip install "mcp[cli]"). Not run. The shape follows the SDK's FastMCP examples. Check the current SDK README, because APIs moved with the 2026-07-28 spec.

# Not run.
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("fund-data")

@mcp.tool()
def get_nav(isin: str, date: str) -> dict:
    """Return the published NAV of a fund plan (ISIN) on a date (YYYY-MM-DD)."""
    nav = lookup_nav(isin, date)           # your read-only data access
    if nav is None:
        raise ValueError("No NAV for that ISIN and date")
    return {"isin": isin, "date": date, "nav": nav}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")   # or "stdio" for a local tool

The SDK's docs recommend Streamable HTTP for production, with stateless and JSON-response options for scale.

C# / .NET: the official C# SDK is published on NuGet as ModelContextProtocol, and it integrates with ASP.NET Core hosting. I couldn't confirm its current attribute and method names here, so follow the SDK repository's samples (github.com/modelcontextprotocol/csharp-sdk).

Testing: the MCP Inspector connects to a server, lists tools and lets you call them by hand.

3.4 Using MCP servers from a model API

Option How
Remote server, called by the API provider Claude's MCP connector (beta): pass mcp_servers plus an mcp_toolset entry, as below
Local or custom server, called by your code An MCP client session in your app, with each tool converted for the model. The Anthropic Python SDK has helpers (anthropic[mcp])
Desktop and IDE clients Add the server in the client's MCP settings 
# Not run: Claude's MCP connector, a beta feature.
response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    betas=["mcp-client-2025-11-20"],
    mcp_servers=[{"type": "url", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp", "name": "fund-data"}],
    tools=[{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "fund-data"}],   # both halves are required
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What was the NAV of INF000X01AB1 on 2026-10-23?"}],
)

4. Working code

The script answers tools/list and tools/call as plain JSON-RPC 2.0, so you can see the message shapes without an SDK. It is a teaching model, not a spec-complete server. Standard library only.

import json

# The shape of MCP's two core tool methods, as plain JSON-RPC 2.0, without any SDK.
# This is a teaching model of the message flow, not a spec-complete server: a real server uses an
# official SDK, which handles transports, versions, capabilities, auth and errors for you.
NAV = {("INF000X01AB1", "2026-10-23"): 142.85}
TOOLS = [{
    "name": "get_nav",
    "description": "Published NAV of a fund plan (ISIN) on a date.",
    "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": False, "required": ["isin", "date"],
                    "properties": {"isin": {"type": "string"}, "date": {"type": "string"}}},
}]

def handle(raw):
    req = json.loads(raw)
    rid, method, params = req.get("id"), req.get("method"), req.get("params", {})
    if method == "tools/list":
        result = {"tools": TOOLS}
    elif method == "tools/call":
        args = params.get("arguments", {})
        if params.get("name") != "get_nav":
            return json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "error": {"code": -32602, "message": "unknown tool"}})
        nav = NAV.get((args.get("isin"), args.get("date")))
        if nav is None:   # a tool-level failure is a normal result flagged isError, so the model can react
            result = {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "No NAV for that ISIN and date."}], "isError": True}
        else:
            result = {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"NAV {nav}"}],
                      "structuredContent": {"isin": args["isin"], "date": args["date"], "nav": nav}}
    else:
        return json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "method not found"}})
    return json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "result": result})

for request in [
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_nav", "arguments": {"isin": "INF000X01AB1", "date": "2026-10-23"}}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_nav", "arguments": {"isin": "INF000X01AB1", "date": "2026-10-24"}}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "method": "prompts/run"},
]:
    print("->", json.dumps(request))
    print("<-", handle(json.dumps(request)))

Output:

-> {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}
<- {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {"tools": [{"name": "get_nav", "description": "Published NAV of a fund plan (ISIN) on a date.", "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false, "required": ["isin", "date"], "properties": {"isin": {"type": "string"}, "date": {"type": "string"}}}}]}}
-> {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_nav", "arguments": {"isin": "INF000X01AB1", "date": "2026-10-23"}}}
<- {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "result": {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "NAV 142.85"}], "structuredContent": {"isin": "INF000X01AB1", "date": "2026-10-23", "nav": 142.85}}}
-> {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_nav", "arguments": {"isin": "INF000X01AB1", "date": "2026-10-24"}}}
<- {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "result": {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "No NAV for that ISIN and date."}], "isError": true}}
-> {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "method": "prompts/run"}
<- {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "method not found"}}

What to notice:

  • tools/list returns the schema the model will see. Write the description for the model.
  • A missing NAV is a normal result with isError: true, not a protocol error. The model can then tell the user or try another date.
  • An unknown method is a JSON-RPC error (-32601). Protocol errors are for broken requests, and tool errors are for things the model can act on.
  • structuredContent gives the host machine-readable data alongside the text.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Vague tool descriptions. The model picks tools by reading them.
  2. Throwing protocol errors for business failures. Return isError results the model can handle.
  3. Session state on the server. The 2026-07-28 core is stateless, so pass explicit handles instead.
  4. Token passthrough and super-user access. Authenticate per request and use the caller's permissions.
  5. Copying a 2025 tutorial. The handshake, sessions and some headers changed. Check the current spec and SDK.

6. Exercise (2 hours)

  1. Add a list_schemes tool to the script, with an amc filter, and a resource nav://{isin}/{date}.
  2. Build the same server with the Python SDK, run it with Streamable HTTP, and call it from the MCP Inspector.
  3. Connect it to a model through the MCP connector (or the SDK helpers), and ask a question that needs two tool calls.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What are MCP's three server capability types?
  2. What is the difference between isError results and JSON-RPC errors?
  3. What did the 2026-07-28 specification change at its core?
  4. Which transport should a remote production server use?
  5. What two parameters does Claude's MCP connector need together?

Answers

  1. Tools, resources and prompts.
  2. isError reports a tool-level failure the model can react to. JSON-RPC errors report malformed or unsupported requests.
  3. It moved to a stateless request and response core (no handshake or sessions, per migration guides), with cacheable lists and hardened authorization.
  4. Streamable HTTP, run stateless, behind normal HTTP infrastructure.
  5. mcp_servers (the server URL and name) and a tools entry of type mcp_toolset naming that server, plus the beta flag.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-27 through web search.

  • The 2026-07-28 specification (official blog): https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/
  • MCP versioning: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/versioning
  • MCP tools (2025-11-25 spec, for the tool shape): https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
  • Migration guide (secondary): https://www.developersdigest.tech/blog/mcp-2026-07-28-breaking-changes
  • Stateless MCP on Azure App Service (Microsoft): https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/appsonazureblog/mcp-just-went-stateless-%E2%80%94-what-the-2026-spec-changes-about-scaling-on-app-servic/4530222
  • Python SDK: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk
  • C# SDK: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/csharp-sdk
  • Claude MCP connector: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector
